lessonInput.title: Relative dating rules
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: Relative dating orders geological events by interpreting relationships such as superposition, inclusions, and cross-cutting without assigning numerical ages. Claim 1: In an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, superposition places older layers below younger layers. Claim 2: A feature that cuts across or disrupts another geological feature must be younger than the feature it disrupts.
lessonInput.readings: Steven Earle, Physical Geology – 2nd Edition (2019), section 8.2, BCcampus Open Education

claims: Relative dating orders geological events by interpreting relationships such as superposition, inclusions, and cross-cutting without assigning numerical ages.
In an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, superposition places older layers below younger layers.
A feature that cuts across or disrupts another geological feature must be younger than the feature it disrupts.

attribution: Steven Earle, Physical Geology – 2nd Edition (2019), section 8.2, BCcampus Open Education

facts: Relative dating orders geological events without assigning numerical ages.
Superposition in undisturbed sedimentary layers places older beds below younger beds.
Cross-cutting features are younger than the rocks or structures they cut.
Inclusions are older than the rock that contains them.
Relative dating compares relationships among layers, cuts, and disruptions to sequence events.

keyTerms.df: Relative dating is a method for arranging geological events by relationships, not by numerical age.
keyTerms.eg: A geologist compares a fault, a lava layer, and sediment beds to order them.
keyTerms.mi: Relative dating means calculating the exact age of each rock layer.
keyTerms.cx: That is incorrect because the method establishes sequence from relationships, not exact numbers.

keyTerms.df: Superposition is the principle that, in an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, lower layers formed earlier than higher layers.
keyTerms.eg: In a flat sediment stack, the lowest mudstone bed predates the sandstone above it.
keyTerms.mi: Superposition says the top layer in a stack is always the oldest.
keyTerms.cx: That reverses the sequence; in undisturbed layers, lower beds are older than higher ones.

keyTerms.df: Cross-cutting describes a feature that disrupts another feature and therefore formed later than what it cuts.
keyTerms.eg: A fracture slicing through several beds must be younger than those beds.
keyTerms.mi: Cross-cutting means the cutting feature must be older because it appears narrower.
keyTerms.cx: Narrowness does not set age; cutting or disruption shows the cutter formed after the cut rock.

scenario.su: A field notebook shows flat sedimentary beds with a narrow fault trace slicing upward through three layers. The team must decide which feature formed first, but no numerical ages are available.
scenario.ma: The notebook sketch shows the fault line crossing the beds, a note that the strata are undisturbed, and a lower shale bed beneath a sandstone bed; students compare the fault trace, the layer order, and the undisturbed sequence.

mc.q: A sketch shows an undisturbed stack of sedimentary beds, with a thin basalt layer inserted near the top and a fault cutting through all beds. Which statement best matches relative dating?
op: The top bed is older than the lower beds because it lies closest to the surface.
The basalt layer must be older than every bed because it is thinner than the others.
The fault is older than the beds because it appears to slice the stack cleanly.
The lowest bed is older than the beds above it, and the fault is younger than every bed it cuts.
mc.ex: Relative dating uses relationships, so lower beds in an undisturbed stack are older, and a cutting fault is younger than the beds it disrupts. The thin basalt layer being inserted does not make it older.

mc.q: A shale bed contains pebbles of sandstone, and a nearby fracture cuts through the shale and pebble-rich layer. With no numerical ages, which interpretation fits the records best?
op: The pebble-rich layer must be the youngest because it is inside another rock.
The shale is older than the pebbles because it surrounds them.
The fracture is older than the shale because it appears in a narrow line.
The pebbles are older than the shale that contains them, and the fracture is younger than both.
mc.ex: Inclusions are older than the rock that contains them, so the sandstone pebbles predate the shale. The fracture is younger than the layers it cuts, whereas being narrow does not make it older.

facts: Superposition in an undisturbed sedimentary sequence dictates that older layers must be situated beneath younger layers.
A feature that cuts across another geological feature must be younger than the feature it disrupts.
In an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, superposition places older layers below younger layers.
In an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, superposition places older layers below younger layers.
A feature that cuts across or disrupts another geological feature must be younger than the feature it disrupts.

keyTerms.df: Superposition is the principle stating that in an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, older layers are found beneath younger layers.
keyTerms.eg: A layer of sandstone is found directly beneath a layer of shale in a rock formation.
keyTerms.mi: Superposition means that the oldest rock is always the one that is physically on top of the younger rock.
keyTerms.cx: Superposition means that the oldest rock is always found beneath the younger rock in an undisturbed sequence.

keyTerms.df: Cross-cutting describes a geological feature that physically cuts across or disrupts another existing geological feature.
keyTerms.eg: A fault line cuts through a layer of sandstone, indicating the fault is younger than the sandstone.
keyTerms.mi: Cross-cutting only applies to features that are horizontal and do not interact with other rock units.
keyTerms.cx: Cross-cutting applies to any feature that physically cuts across or disrupts another geological feature, regardless of its orientation.

keyTerms.df: Relative dating is the process of ordering geological events by interpreting relationships like superposition and cross-cutting without assigning numerical ages.
keyTerms.eg: Using superposition and cross-cutting, one can determine which rock layer formed first.
keyTerms.mi: Relative dating requires assigning absolute numerical ages to all geological events to establish a timeline.
keyTerms.cx: Relative dating involves ordering events by interpreting relationships like superposition and cross-cutting without assigning numerical ages.

scenario.su: A geologist examines a rock outcrop where a dike cuts through a sequence of sedimentary layers. The dike is clearly younger than the surrounding layers, and the sedimentary layers show clear layering. The constraint is that the geologist must only use the observed relationships to determine the relative ages.
scenario.ma: The geologist observes a dike cutting across a layer of sandstone and shale. The sedimentary layers show clear layering, and the dike is clearly younger than the surrounding layers.

mc.q: When observing a sequence, if a feature cuts across another, what relationship must be established between the two features regarding their age?
op: The feature that cuts across must be older than the feature it disrupts.
The feature that cuts across must be younger than the feature it disrupts.
The feature that cuts across must be the same age as the feature it disrupts.
The feature that cuts across must be completely unrelated to the feature it disrupts.
mc.ex: A feature that cuts across or disrupts another geological feature must be younger than the feature it disrupts, which supports the correct option, while the other options suggest incorrect age relationships.

mc.q: Given the observation of a sedimentary sequence, how does the principle of superposition help determine the relative ages of the layers?
op: Superposition indicates that the youngest layer is always found at the bottom of the sequence.
Superposition indicates that older layers are found below younger layers in an undisturbed sequence.
Superposition only applies to igneous rocks and does not affect sedimentary sequences.
Superposition only applies when features are cross-cutting each other, not when layers are stacked.
mc.ex: In an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, superposition places older layers below younger layers, which supports the correct option, while the other options suggest incorrect vertical ordering.
